title: Re'eh: the release (Deuteronomy 15:1–2)
hookLine: every seventh year debts are released

cards: Picture the moment a student loan is finally paid off, or a medical bill forgiven. People describe it with their bodies. I could breathe again.
A weight off my chest. Now imagine that moment built into the calendar. Every seven years, for everyone, at once.
Not because a bank decided to be kind, but because the law said so. That's the seventh year in Deuteronomy. And the Mishnah remembers what happened when people actually tried to live by it.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release." The Hebrew word is shmita, a letting drop.

Exodus already used that verb for the land: in the seventh year, let it drop, let it lie fallow. Deuteronomy uses it for debts. Each creditor lets go of what he lent to his neighbor, and doesn't press for it.
Debt piles up. Without a reset, the poor get poorer and people get trapped.

teach.h: A RESET FOR A WHOLE SOCIETY.
teach.b: The release lets a whole society start over. But the Torah knows people. A few verses later it warns: don't let a base thought into your heart, saying the seventh year is close, and refuse to lend.
If every loan will be wiped out in a year, why lend? By the time of Hillel, around the turn of the common era, that's what people were doing.
The Mishnah says he saw that people had stopped lending to one another, and the poor were the ones getting hurt.
So Hillel created a legal document called the prozbul.

A lender could hand his debts over to the court, and debts held by a court weren't released. Lending started again. Some later teachers were uneasy, and the debate about Hillel's fix runs through the Talmud.
But the motive is clear: a law meant to protect the poor had started to hurt them, and Hillel acted to protect them again.

how: In the land of Israel, observant Jewish farmers still keep the shmita year for the land, and many observant Jews sign a prozbul before the end of the seventh year so that loans aren't canceled.

practice: Think of what someone owes you: maybe money, but more often an apology, a favor returned, a call back, credit for something you did. Let one of those debts come to mind, and notice the weight of holding it.
Then ask what it would be like to let this one drop, not because they've earned it, but because the year has turned.
